# Markdown Runs Both Ways

.pull-left[
**What you write for Claude**

- `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/`
- a spec (`learning-plan.md`, `SPEC.md`)
- a brief for an agent or a peer session
- a skill (`SKILL.md`, module 6)
]

.pull-right[
**What Claude writes for you**

- `README.md`, `concepts.md`
- plans and handoff notes
- findings reports from verifier agents
- commit messages
]

--

Both directions have the same failure: a document that **reads well and is wrong**. The module is about writing that cannot drift and checks that catch it when it does.

---
name: facts-not-procedures

# Instruction Files: Facts, Not Procedures

What the docs say, and what experience confirms, about `CLAUDE.md`:

--

**Facts.** Build commands, conventions, layout, "always do X." A multi-step procedure that matters for one kind of task goes in a skill or a path-scoped rule, loaded only when needed.

--

**Under 200 lines.** Every line is paid for on every request, and adherence drops as the file grows. `@imports` organize a long file; they do not make it cheaper. Imported files load at launch too.

--

**Consistent.** Two contradicting lines let the model pick one. `/doctor prompt-audit` finds contradictions and stale entries.

--

**Context, not enforcement.** Everything here is weighed, not obeyed. To make something impossible, write a hook (module 7).

---

# `/init` Writes the Discoverable Half

`/init` reads the codebase and drafts a `CLAUDE.md`: build commands, test commands, conventions it can see. If one exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting.

--

What it cannot discover, and what is worth adding by hand:

- **why** a convention exists ("the CSV is generated; committing it would make every rebuild a diff")
- **what not to do** ("never add `.DS_Store` to a per-repo `.gitignore`; the global excludes file covers it")
- **what "done" means** ("script runs clean, one row per city, bad rows excluded and counted")

--

The drill's target: a `CLAUDE.md` for the practice repo under 40 lines, every line a fact.

---
name: lessons-library

# The Lessons-Library Pattern

A global `CLAUDE.md` that keeps every lesson from every session passes 200 lines within months.

--

What keeps it under control:

.small[
```markdown
# Lessons library: read the matching file BEFORE that kind of task

Playbooks live in ~/.claude/lessons/, one file per area. NOT loaded
automatically. When a task touches an area below, read that whole file first.
When you learn a new lesson in one of these areas, add it there, not here.

- latex.md (18): any LaTeX build, bibtex, page-fitting, latexdiff, TikZ.
- slides-xaringan.md (12): authoring or verifying xaringan decks.
- git-collab.md (16): stash, cross-checks, shared-doc sync, gh auth, hooks.
```
]

--

The writing lesson, separate from the mechanics (module 5): an index line must say **when** to read the file, not just what it contains. "Any LaTeX build" is a trigger; "LaTeX notes" is not.

---

# A Burned Example: Number vs Definition

An instruction read:

> for the 112 cases where control is an empty arm

The empty-arm cases were the other **205**. The number and the definition picked out different sets.

--

The definition is usually the load-bearing intent; the number is the slip.

--

When **writing** a spec: give the definition, let the number be computed.

When **reading** one and the two disagree: surface the contradiction, implement against the definition (per row, not a hardcoded count), confirm before changing anything published. Do not silently pick the number.

---
name: spec-main

# One Document Is the Spec

Every course in this collection has a `learning-plan.md`. The README, the hub page, each module's `concepts.md` are **derived** from it and expected to agree with it.

--

The scaffolding skill reads the plan first and stops if the requested module is not in it.

--

The practice, independent of the file name:

> One document is the spec. Everything else is derived. A disagreement is a bug in the derived document until proven otherwise.

--

In the drill, `SPEC.md` for the practice repo is written **ahead of the code** on purpose: it names an exclusion rule the script does not implement yet. The README then has to say so in a "Known gaps" section rather than describing the script as if it were the spec.

---

# Briefs: The Only Context the Recipient Has

A subagent, a peer session, a cloud session: each starts with nothing but the brief.

--

What works:

- **Goal and what is ruled out.** "Add the exclusion rule from SPEC.md; the median column is already done."
- **Pointers, not retyping.** "Read SPEC.md and data/trip_metrics.R."
- **What to do with the result.** "Commit per chunk, do not push, return a summary as text."
- **Self-contained.** A restarted peer session has a new name and none of the earlier context.

<a href="#brief-scoping" class="nav-btn">a scoping burn →</a>

---

# What Claude Writes: Three Kinds

**README and concepts.** Derived from the spec. Numbers computed from the source, not typed from memory. "24 CSVs" after the pipeline makes 29 is the commonest stale fact.

--

**Plans and handoff notes.** A `NEXT SESSION` block at the end of a session, written to disk: state, rules, build and verify steps, the file boundary for the next session. A conditional thread ("when a cloud session asks") gets one line or is dropped. Once the user dismisses a thread, it stays out of every later recap.

--

**Findings reports.** A verifier agent's output. Save each to disk as it lands. A subagent asked to write a report file is refused ("return findings as text"), so the main session does the writing.

---
name: grep-main

# Facts That Survive `grep`

A README audit for a stale count:

```bash
grep -n "24 CSVs" README.md        # finds nothing...
```

...because the text says:

```
the 24
handoff CSVs
```

--

Line-based search misses a fact wrapped across lines. Same trap in LaTeX: `555~0123` slips past a space-or-hyphen pattern for a phone number.

--

Two habits:

- **Writing:** one fact, one line, one spelling.
- **Auditing:** sweep with the bare number (`grep -nE '\b24\b'`) plus a context pass, or read the whole section. And on this machine `grep` is `ugrep`, which has produced silent false negatives: confirm an "absent" with python `'phrase' in open(f).read()` before concluding.

---

# House Style Belongs in the Instruction File

This collection's `CLAUDE.md` carries a prose style for anything user-facing: no em-dashes, short sentences, few colons and semicolons, no opening affirmations, no filler.

--

Why it lives there instead of being re-explained each session:

- it is a **fact about every task**, which is exactly what the file is for
- it is **checkable**: `grep -c` for the character before a commit, exit code and all

--

```bash
# zero em-dashes is the GOOD result, and grep -c exits 1 on zero:
# chain a commit after it and the commit is skipped. Keep them separate.
perl -CSD -ne 'print "$ARGV:$.: $_" if /\x{2014}/' README.md
```

---

# Summary

| Document | Written by | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `CLAUDE.md` | you (+ `/init`) | facts, under 200 lines, audited for contradictions |
| playbook files | you | one per area, index line says *when* to read |
| spec | you | one source of truth; everything else derived |
| brief | you | goal, pointers, scoped rules, what to return |
| README / concepts | Claude | derived from the spec; numbers computed, one per line |
| handoff note | Claude | on disk, state + rules + verify steps + file boundary |
| findings | agent, saved by main | to disk as they land |

--

The drill builds all of the "you" rows for the practice repo and audits the first "Claude" row.

name: brief-scoping

# Backup: A Scoping Burn (2026-09)

.small[
A brief to a peer session said:

> Don't name any school.

Meant: the school being applied to. Read as: every institution. The peer stripped three universities from a web page, all of them true affiliations the source kept.

The fix is in the writing:

> Don't name X, Y, Z (the target). Other affiliations stay as in the source. Citations of that faculty's published work are fine.

Two more from the same family:

- Before asking a peer to "restore" something, check the diff. One "missing" item had never been on the page; the request was really an addition.
- From the receiving side: when a relayed rule would delete real content, ask for its exact scope before stripping anything.
]
